englit_ocr.2.0.summary: Animal Farm was written by George Orwell in 1945 as a satirical critique of totalitarianism, drawing on the Russian Revolution and Stalinist regime. The social, historical and literary contexts shape the novel’s allegorical structure, characterisation and language, allowing Orwell to expose the corrupting nature of power and the manipulation of language.

core.h: Historical Context – The Russian Revolution & Stalinism
core.p: Orwell wrote Animal Farm after witnessing the 1917 Russian Revolution and the subsequent rise of Joseph Stalin, whose regime became synonymous with totalitarian oppression. The novel mirrors the trajectory from revolutionary idealism to authoritarian rule, using the farm as a micro‑cosm of Soviet society.
bullets: 1917 Bolshevik Revolution – overthrow of Tsarist autocracy
Stalin’s consolidation of power – purges, collectivisation, cult of personality
1945 – post‑war disillusionment and the spread of communism
Orwell’s own experiences – 1933 Spanish Civil War, anti‑totalitarian stance

callouts.p: A system of government that centralises power in a single authority, suppressing dissent and controlling all aspects of public and private life.
The systematic elimination of perceived enemies, exemplified by the Great Purge (1936‑38), which Orwell critiques through the execution of animals.

core.h: Social Context – Class Struggle & Ideological Manipulation
core.p: The novel reflects the class tensions in Britain and the manipulation of language by political elites to maintain control. Orwell’s depiction of the pigs’ gradual usurpation of the farm’s resources parallels the exploitation of the working class.
bullets: Working‑class aspirations – desire for equality and better living conditions
Propaganda – slogans like “All animals are equal” used to justify oppression
Language as a tool of power – the pigs’ alteration of commandments
The ‘revolutionary’ rhetoric that becomes hypocritical

callouts.t: Remember to link language change to power shift
callouts.p: Show how the pigs’ rewriting of the Seven Commandments mirrors real‑world propaganda.

core.h: Literary Context – Satire & Allegory in 20th Century Literature
core.p: Animal Farm is a classic example of political satire and allegory, following in the tradition of Jonathan Swift and George Orwell’s own earlier work, Homage to Catalonia.
bullets: Satire – using humour, irony and exaggeration to critique power
Allegory – characters represent real historical figures (e.g., Napoleon = Stalin)
Realism vs. fantasy – the farm’s realistic setting juxtaposed with fantastical animal speech
Orwell’s clear, concise prose – a hallmark of his style

callouts.p: A narrative that uses symbolic characters and events to represent real‑world ideas or people.
Allegory is a whole narrative; metaphor is a single comparison.

core.h: Impact of Context on Text – Structure & Narrative Technique
core.p: Orwell structures the novel in five parts, each mirroring a stage of the Soviet Union’s development. The use of a simple, almost childlike narrative voice heightens the contrast between the farm’s innocence and the pigs’ corruption.
bullets: Five parts – 1) Rebellion, 2) Early reforms, 3) Consolidation, 4) Betrayal, 5) Final state
Narrative voice – omniscient, detached, yet sympathetic to the animals
Foreshadowing – the windmill’s repeated promise of progress
Parallelism – repetition of the Seven Commandments to show erosion of ideals

callouts.t: Use the five‑part structure to organise your essay
callouts.p: Explain each part’s historical parallel before analysing its literary effect.

core.h: Language & Rhetoric – The Power of Slogans
core.p: The repeated slogan “All animals are equal” and its eventual alteration to “All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others” illustrate how language can be weaponised to justify inequality.
bullets: Slogans – simple, memorable, easily manipulated
Repetition – reinforces ideology
Irony – the final commandment subverts the original ideal
Propaganda – the pigs’ use of language to control the herd

callouts.p: Information, ideas or images deliberately spread to influence public opinion, often biased or misleading.

core.p: While Animal Farm is an allegory, Orwell deliberately simplifies complex events to focus on the moral lesson. He uses animal characters to universalise the experience of oppression, making the story accessible to a broad audience.
bullets: Simplification – complex political events condensed into farm dynamics
Universalisation – animals represent all oppressed peoples
Artistic licence – exaggerated traits (e.g., Napoleon’s pig‑face) to heighten satire
Historical fidelity – key events (e.g., the windmill, the purge) remain recognisable

callouts.t: Highlight the balance between allegory and realism
callouts.p: Show how Orwell keeps the narrative grounded while using allegory to comment on real events.

core.h: Exam Relevance – What Mark Schemes Look For
core.p: Mark schemes reward explicit links between context and text, use of terminology, and analysis of how context shapes characterisation, structure and language.
bullets: Contextual knowledge – dates, events, figures
Terminology – satire, allegory, propaganda, totalitarianism
Textual evidence – quotations of commandments, slogans
Analysis – explain why Orwell made specific choices
Structure – clear introduction, body, conclusion

callouts.p: A set of criteria used by examiners to award marks for each answer.

core.p: Students often misinterpret allegory, overlook historical details, or fail to link context to literary devices. Avoid these by checking each answer against the spec.
bullets: Confusing allegory with metaphor
Ignoring the five‑part structure
Failing to cite specific historical events
Over‑generalising language changes without evidence

callouts.t: Don’t just list facts – analyse their impact
callouts.p: Show how each historical detail influences the narrative.

analogy.p: Imagine the farm as a factory where the pigs are the managers. Initially, everyone works together, but the managers gradually take more control, change the rules, and keep the workers’ labour for themselves. The factory’s machinery (the windmill) promises progress but is used to exploit workers. This analogy helps explain the shift from equality to inequality, but it breaks down when you consider that the animals can speak and that the narrative is a satirical allegory, not a literal factory.

terms.d: A narrative that uses symbolic characters and events to represent real‑world ideas or people.
A literary technique that uses humour, irony or exaggeration to criticise or expose.
A system of government that centralises power in a single authority, suppressing dissent and controlling all aspects of life.
Information deliberately spread to influence public opinion, often biased or misleading.
A sudden, fundamental change in political power or social structure.
The political practice of building a heroic image of a leader.
Symbolic of industrial progress and the promise of a better future.
The Seven Rules that govern the farm, which are gradually altered.
A literary device that hints at future events.
A contrast between expectation and reality.

mistakes.r: Define propaganda and show how the pigs use slogans.

mistakes.w: I didn't mention the five parts of the novel
mistakes.r: The structure mirrors stages of the Soviet Union and must be referenced.

mistakes.r: Explain its symbolic meaning for progress and exploitation.

exam.q: Compare the use of slogans in Animal Farm with a modern political slogan of your choice.
model: Identify a modern slogan (e.g., “Make America Great Again”).
Analyse its structure and purpose.

exam.tip: Use clear comparison points: structure, purpose, effect.

worked.q: Write a paragraph analysing how the alteration of the Seven Commandments reflects the erosion of revolutionary ideals.
steps: Introduce the Seven Commandments as the farm’s moral code.
Quote the original commandment: ‘All animals are equal.’
Show the alteration to ‘All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others.’
Explain how this change mirrors the Soviet elite’s hypocrisy.
Conclude with the impact on the herd’s trust.
worked.ans: The Seven Commandments are the farm’s moral code, beginning with the idealistic ‘All animals are equal.’ As the pigs consolidate power, they alter it to ‘All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others,’ mirroring the Soviet elite’s hypocrisy and eroding the original revolutionary ideals, ultimately breaking the herd’s trust.

englit_ocr.2.3.summary: Animal Farm explores how power corrupts, the manipulation of truth, and the loss of freedom, showing that revolutions can become the very tyranny they opposed. The novel’s themes are interwoven through characters, language, and structure, making it a rich text for exam analysis.

core.p: Orwell shows that those who gain power often become corrupt, turning the original ideals of the revolution into oppressive rule.
bullets: - The pigs’ gradual takeover mirrors real political shifts
- Squealer’s propaganda demonstrates manipulation of truth
- The final line, “All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others,” encapsulates the betrayal of equality

callouts.p: Power corrupts because it isolates leaders from the people’s needs.
Show how the pigs’ actions change from equality to tyranny.

core.h: Theme 2 – Manipulation of Truth and Language
core.p: Orwell uses language as a tool of control, illustrating how truth can be reshaped to serve those in power.
bullets: - The Seven Commandments are altered to justify actions
- Squealer’s speeches reframe events to maintain loyalty
- The use of propaganda slogans like ‘Four legs good, two legs bad’

callouts.p: Information, ideas, or images used to influence public opinion.
Do not conflate propaganda with general rhetoric; it is specifically designed to manipulate.

core.h: Theme 3 – Loss of Freedom and Individuality
core.p: The novel shows how the promise of freedom is eroded as the pigs consolidate control, reducing animals to mere workers.
bullets: - The farm’s laws become stricter
- The animals are forced to work harder
- The final scene shows the pigs indistinguishable from humans

callouts.p: Link the loss of freedom to the pigs’ increasing human traits.

core.p: Orwell suggests that revolutions often repeat the same patterns of oppression, warning readers of the dangers of unchecked ambition.
bullets: - The farm’s initial rebellion mirrors the Russian Revolution
- The final outcome mirrors the original oppressive regime
- The pigs’ rise echoes the very tyrants they overthrew

callouts.p: The pattern where a new regime replicates the oppression of its predecessor.

core.h: Theme 5 – The Role of Education and Literacy
core.p: Education is portrayed as a double-edged sword; while it can empower, it can also be used to indoctrinate.
bullets: - The pigs’ literacy gives them advantage
- The other animals’ ignorance keeps them compliant
- Squealer’s speeches rely on the animals’ limited understanding

callouts.p: Discuss how literacy creates a power imbalance.

core.p: Orwell blurs the line between human and animal, showing that the nature of tyranny is universal.
bullets: - The pigs’ final resemblance to humans
- The animals’ loss of distinct identity
- The moral of the story applies to all societies

callouts.p: The pigs become indistinguishable from humans, symbolising the universality of tyranny.

analogy.t: Orwell’s farm as a political stage
analogy.p: Like a theatre where actors (pigs) gradually take the director’s role, the audience (animals) becomes passive. The analogy breaks when the actors become the director’s costume, blurring performer and production.

terms.d: Information or ideas used to influence public opinion, often misleading.
Original rules of Animal Farm, altered to justify the pigs’ actions.
Pig who manipulates language to control the other animals.
Pattern where a new regime replicates the oppression of its predecessor.
A set of beliefs that justifies the actions of those in power.
Using ideology to control or justify actions.
Political system where the state holds absolute power.
Deliberate misrepresentation of truth.

mistakes.w: Power corrupts because it is absolute
mistakes.r: Power corrupts because it isolates leaders from the people’s needs.

mistakes.w: Propaganda is just persuasive speech
mistakes.r: Propaganda is specifically designed to manipulate public opinion.

mistakes.w: The pigs are just better at farming
mistakes.r: They use farming skills to justify political control.

mistakes.w: The animals are free after the rebellion
mistakes.r: They lose freedom as the pigs consolidate power.

mistakes.w: The novel is a simple story about farm animals
mistakes.r: It is an allegory about political power and manipulation.

model: The pigs’ transformation shows the cycle of revolution.
It illustrates that those who gain power can become the very oppressors they opposed.
exam.tip: Focus on the symbolism of the pigs’ human traits.

exam.q: Explain how the theme of manipulation of truth is presented through language in Animal Farm.
model: The pigs alter the Seven Commandments.
Squealer’s speeches reframe events.
The animals’ limited literacy allows manipulation.
exam.tip: Link language changes to the pigs’ consolidation of power.

model: The farm’s laws become stricter.
The animals are forced to work harder.
The final scene shows the pigs indistinguishable from humans.
exam.tip: Show the progression from equality to oppression.

englit_ocr.2.4.summary: Animal Farm’s language, form and structure are deliberately crafted to mirror the rise of totalitarianism, using simple, allegorical prose, a clear narrative arc, and a range of rhetorical devices that reinforce the novel’s critique of power and propaganda.

core.p: Orwell structures the novel as a linear progression from revolutionary idealism to authoritarian corruption, mirroring the historical trajectory of the Russian Revolution. The plot is divided into five parts, each representing a stage of the farm’s political evolution.
bullets: Part 1 – The Rebellion: introduction of characters, setting, and the Seven Commandments.
Part 2 – Consolidation of Power: Snowball’s expulsion, the building of the windmill, and the first alterations to the commandments.
Part 3 – The Windmill’s Demise: Napoleon’s betrayal, the destruction of the windmill, and the beginning of the pigs’ moral decay.
Part 4 – The Final Transformation: the pigs’ adoption of human habits, the removal of the commandments, and the final equality of all animals to humans.
Part 5 – The Closing Scene: the pigs’ secret meetings and the animals’ realization of their oppression.

callouts.p: The five parts correspond to the stages of political change: Rebellion, Consolidation, Betrayal, Transformation, and Realisation.

core.p: Orwell’s diction is deliberately simple yet loaded with symbolic meaning, allowing the novel to function as a universal critique of totalitarian regimes.
bullets: Use of animal names to represent historical figures (e.g., Napoleon = Stalin, Snowball = Trotsky).
The Seven Commandments as a flexible moral code that is progressively amended.
The windmill as a symbol of industrial progress and propaganda.
The pigs’ gradual adoption of human traits (walking on two legs, wearing clothes) to illustrate the erosion of revolutionary ideals.

callouts.p: A narrative that uses symbolic characters and events to represent real-world issues.
Mark every instance where a symbol is altered or used to convey a political message.

core.p: Orwell employs a range of rhetorical devices to reinforce the novel’s themes and to manipulate the reader’s perception of the pigs’ regime.
bullets: Repetition – the commandment “All animals are equal” is echoed throughout, highlighting hypocrisy.
Irony – the pigs’ claim of equality while they enjoy privileges.
Metonymy – the use of “the pigs” to represent the ruling class.
Allusion – references to the Russian Revolution and Soviet propaganda.
Paradox – “The more we work, the less we have” to show the futility of the regime’s promises.

callouts.p: A contrast between what is said and what is meant, often to expose hypocrisy.
Sarcasm is a form of irony but is usually directed at a person; here it is used to expose systemic hypocrisy.

core.h: Narrative Point of View and Reliability
core.p: The novel is narrated in third-person limited, focusing on the animals’ perspective, which creates an unreliable account that mirrors propaganda.
bullets: Third-person limited allows the narrator to present the animals’ naive understanding of events.
The narrator’s tone shifts from hopeful to cynical, reflecting the animals’ loss of faith.
The unreliability of the narrator parallels the manipulation of information by the regime.

callouts.p: A narrator whose credibility is compromised, often due to bias or limited knowledge.

core.p: Dialogue is used to reveal character motives, to disseminate propaganda, and to create a sense of community that is later fractured.
bullets: The pigs’ speeches are persuasive, using simple slogans to manipulate the other animals.
The animals’ conversations often reveal their ignorance and willingness to accept propaganda.
The use of direct speech in the final scene underscores the betrayal of the original ideals.

callouts.p: Note the use of short, declarative sentences in propaganda versus longer, reflective sentences in dissent.

core.p: Each chapter is a self-contained episode that collectively builds the narrative’s moral trajectory.
bullets: Chapters are numbered but not titled, reflecting the uniformity of the regime.
The progression of chapters mirrors the erosion of the Seven Commandments.
The final chapter’s lack of resolution emphasizes the cyclical nature of oppression.

callouts.p: The absence of chapter titles reinforces the loss of individuality and the imposition of a single narrative.

core.p: The triple-only content for this point includes the use of the Seven Commandments, the windmill, and the pigs’ transformation into humans.
bullets: The Seven Commandments are altered three times, each time reflecting a shift in power.
The windmill is built, destroyed, and rebuilt, symbolising the regime’s manipulation of progress.
The pigs’ final transformation into humans is a direct parallel to the original oppressors.

callouts.p: Content that is only rewarded at the higher tier of the exam.

analogy.p: Imagine the farm as a factory where the workers (animals) are fed a simple, repetitive slogan (the commandment) that keeps them productive. Over time, the managers (pigs) start to wear the same uniforms as the factory owners, blurring the line between worker and owner. The analogy works to show the gradual loss of identity but breaks down when the factory’s machinery (the windmill) is destroyed and rebuilt, a step that cannot be captured by a simple factory model.

terms.d: A narrative that uses symbolic characters and events to represent real-world issues.
A narrator whose credibility is compromised, often due to bias or limited knowledge.
A contrast between what is said and what is meant, often to expose hypocrisy.
A figure of speech in which a thing is called by the name of something closely associated with it.
Information, ideas, or rumors deliberately spread to influence public opinion.
The original laws of Animal Farm, which are progressively altered to justify the pigs’ actions.
A symbol of industrial progress and the regime’s manipulation of hope.
Content that is only rewarded at the higher tier of the exam.

englit_ocr.2.1.summary: Animal Farm is a satirical novella that follows a group of farm animals who overthrow their human owner, only to find themselves ruled by a new tyranny. The plot is divided into five distinct stages—revolution, consolidation of power, betrayal, oppression, and the erosion of ideals—each marked by key events that mirror the rise and fall of totalitarian regimes. The structure is linear and cyclical, ending with the animals’ loss of freedom and the complete subversion of the original revolutionary ideals. Understanding this progression is essential for analysing the text’s themes, characters and the author’s critique of power.

core.p: Animal Farm’s plot follows a clear, five‑stage arc that mirrors the historical trajectory of a totalitarian state. Each stage is defined by a pivotal event that shifts the power balance and reveals the underlying themes of corruption and manipulation.
bullets: • **Stage 1 – The Rebellion**: The animals overthrow Mr. Jones, establishing a new order based on equality.
• **Stage 2 – The Consolidation of Power**: Napoleon’s pigs assume leadership, rewriting the Seven Commandments to suit their needs.
• **Stage 3 – The Betrayal**: The pigs begin to trade with humans, breaking the original principles of Animalism.
• **Stage 4 – The Oppression**: The farm’s conditions deteriorate; the pigs enjoy luxuries while the other animals suffer.
• **Stage 5 – The Erosion of Ideals**: The final commandment is altered to “All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others.”

callouts.p: Remember the five stages and the key event that defines each.

core.p: A visual timeline helps to place events in chronological order and shows the progression from idealism to cynicism.
bullets: • 1st Day – Rebellion and the Seven Commandments
• 1st Month – Napoleon’s coup and the pigs’ rise
• 3rd Month – The first trade with humans
• 6th Month – The destruction of the windmill
• 12th Month – The final commandment change

core.p: The story is narrated in the third person limited, focusing on the animals’ collective experience while allowing the reader to see the pigs’ manipulation of language and truth.
bullets: • **Third person limited** gives an objective yet intimate view.
• The narrator’s tone shifts from hopeful to cynical, mirroring the farm’s decline.
• The use of the animals’ own language (e.g., the Seven Commandments) highlights the manipulation of truth.

callouts.p: A narrator who knows the thoughts and feelings of one or a few characters, but not all.

core.p: Orwell employs several structural techniques to reinforce the theme of propaganda and control.
bullets: • **Repetition of the Seven Commandments**: shows how slogans are altered.
• **Circular structure**: the ending mirrors the beginning, with the pigs indistinguishable from humans.
• **Foreshadowing**: the windmill’s destruction foreshadows the loss of hope.

core.p: Each structural element is deliberately placed to illustrate the erosion of revolutionary ideals.
bullets: • **Early optimism**: the windmill’s construction represents progress.
• **Mid‑stage corruption**: the pigs’ trade deals show betrayal.
• **Final cynicism**: the commandment change signals total subversion.

core.p: The plot’s stages correspond closely to the rise of the Soviet Union, providing a historical lens for analysis.
bullets: • **Rebellion** → 1917 Russian Revolution
• **Consolidation** → 1920s Stalinist purges
• **Betrayal** → 1930s collectivisation
• **Oppression** → 1940s war hardships
• **Erosion** → 1950s Khrushchev’s revelations

core.h: 7. Exam‑Ready Summary of Plot and Structure
core.p: Remember the five stages, key events, and how structure mirrors the rise and fall of power. Use the timeline and thematic links to support any answer.
bullets: • Five stages: Rebellion, Consolidation, Betrayal, Oppression, Erosion
• Key events: Seven Commandments, Windmill, Trade, Commandment change
• Structure: linear, circular, repetitive slogans
• Thematic link: idealism → corruption → cynicism

analogy.t: The Farm as a Political Machine
analogy.p: Imagine a factory that starts with a fair assembly line but gradually becomes run by a few managers who change the rules to favour themselves. The factory’s machinery (the windmill) is built for efficiency, yet the managers (the pigs) repurpose it for profit, ultimately making the workers (the other animals) invisible. The analogy works until the factory’s purpose shifts from production to profit; at that point, the factory no longer reflects the original democratic ideals.

terms.d: The original laws set by the animals to guide their society, later altered to justify the pigs’ actions.
Narrative perspective focusing on the thoughts and feelings of a single character or group.
A narrative that ends where it began, often to emphasize a theme.
Hints or clues about future events.
Information used to influence opinions, often by manipulating language.
The gradual loss or distortion of original principles.
The act of overthrowing an existing authority.
The process by which a leader or group strengthens control.
The act of breaking a promise or principle.
The exercise of authority in a harsh or unjust way.

mistakes.w: The plot is just a simple story about animals fighting a human.
mistakes.r: The plot is a political allegory about the rise and fall of totalitarian regimes.

mistakes.w: The windmill is built to help the animals farm better.
mistakes.r: The windmill is a symbol of hope and progress that is ultimately destroyed.

mistakes.w: The pigs become human because they physically turn into humans.
mistakes.r: The pigs become indistinguishable from humans through behaviour and language.

mistakes.w: The Seven Commandments are never changed.
mistakes.r: The Seven Commandments are repeatedly altered to justify the pigs’ actions.

exam.q: Explain how the structure of Animal Farm reflects the theme of propaganda.
model: - The story is divided into five stages that mirror the rise and fall of a totalitarian state.
- The Seven Commandments are repeated and altered, showing how slogans are manipulated.
- The circular structure (ending with the pigs as humans) emphasises the subversion of the original ideals.
- Foreshadowing (e.g., the windmill’s destruction) hints at the loss of hope.
exam.tip: Link each structural element to a specific example of propaganda.

exam.q: Describe the significance of the windmill’s destruction in the context of the plot.
model: - The windmill symbolises the animals’ hope and progress.
- Its destruction shows the betrayal of the original ideals and the pigs’ prioritisation of power.
exam.tip: Focus on symbolism rather than literal function.

exam.q: How does Orwell use the narrative perspective to develop the plot?
model: - Third person limited allows the reader to see the animals’ collective experience.
- The narrator’s tone shifts from hopeful to cynical, mirroring the farm’s decline.
- The perspective highlights the manipulation of language by the pigs.
- The limited view keeps the focus on the animals’ loss of freedom.
exam.tip: Analyse the narrator’s tone and its change across the stages.

exam.q: Identify and explain two key events that mark the transition from revolution to tyranny.
model: - Napoleon’s coup and the pigs’ takeover of leadership.
- The first trade with humans, breaking the Seven Commandments.
exam.tip: Use the timeline to support your answer.

exam.q: Compare the ending of Animal Farm with the beginning in terms of the animals’ status.
model: - At the start, the animals are free and equal.
- At the end, the pigs are indistinguishable from humans, showing total subversion.
exam.tip: Use the phrase ‘indistinguishable from humans’.

worked.q: Explain why the windmill is a crucial symbol in the plot.
steps: 1. Identify the windmill as a symbol of hope and progress.
2. Show how its construction represents the animals’ collective effort.
3. Explain its destruction as a betrayal of the original ideals.
4. Relate this to the theme of propaganda and manipulation.
worked.ans: The windmill represents the animals’ hope and collective effort. Its construction shows progress, but its destruction betrays the original ideals, illustrating how propaganda manipulates truth.

englit_ocr.2.5.summary: These notes give a comprehensive, exam‑ready guide to the OCR J352 spec point on *Animal Farm* exam skills. They cover how to compare a studied extract with an unseen modern extract, how to answer a related question on the studied text, and the key techniques and terminology that the mark scheme rewards. The material is structured for quick revision, with colour‑coded headings, bullet lists, tables, callouts, and diagrams where useful. The aim is to equip a student with the depth of analysis and the precise language needed to achieve a grade 9.

core.p: The spec asks you to:
bullets: (a) compare an extract from *Animal Farm* with an unseen modern extract of the same genre, showing how the texts use language, structure and themes to convey similar or different ideas;
(b) answer a related question on the studied text, demonstrating a deep understanding of its literary features and how they support the writer’s purpose.

callouts.p: The ability to analyse and compare texts, and to answer questions that test knowledge of the studied text.

core.p: Use these terms exactly as they appear in the mark scheme.
bullets: **Language** – the words, phrases and stylistic devices used.
**Structure** – the organisation of the text (e.g. narrative, dialogue, paragraphing).
**Theme** – the underlying ideas explored.
**Characterisation** – how characters are presented and developed.
**Tone** – the writer’s attitude towards the subject.
**Point of view** – the narrative perspective.
**Imagery** – sensory details that create mental pictures.
**Allusion** – a reference to another text or event.

core.p: Follow this sequence to ensure you hit all the criteria.
bullets: 1. Identify the **purpose** of each extract (e.g. to persuade, to inform, to entertain).
2. Analyse the **language**: look for diction, figurative language, rhetorical devices, and the effect they create.
3. Examine the **structure**: how is the extract organised? Note paragraph breaks, dialogue, pacing and any shifts in perspective.
4. Discuss the **themes** and how each extract treats them – are they the same or different?
5. Consider **characterisation**: how are characters introduced or described?
6. Compare the **tone** and **point of view** – does one text feel more cynical, hopeful, etc.?
7. Conclude with a clear statement of how the two extracts are similar or differ in achieving their purpose.

callouts.p: Write a two‑column table with headings for Language, Structure, Theme, Characterisation, Tone, Point of view. Fill in key points for each extract.

core.p: A quick visual aid for exam practice.

More complex syntax; metaphorical language; subtle irony
Paragraphs vary in length; dialogue interspersed

core.p: The spec requires you to answer a question that tests your knowledge of *Animal Farm*’s literary features. Approach it as a mini‑essay:
bullets: State the question’s focus (e.g. characterisation, theme, language).
Identify the relevant passage(s) and the literary device(s) involved.
Explain how the device supports the writer’s purpose and the overall meaning of the text.
Use precise terminology and quote the text where appropriate.
Conclude by linking back to the question’s aim.

callouts.p: A question that asks you to analyse a specific feature of the studied text.
Spend 1‑2 minutes outlining the key points before you write.

core.h: 6. Common Traps and How to Avoid Them
core.p: Mark schemes penalise these mistakes; be vigilant.
bullets: *Over‑generalising* – avoid vague statements like ‘the text is about power’.
*Missing the point* – ensure you answer the exact question asked.
*Incorrect terminology* – use the exact terms from the spec.
*Failing to compare* – in part (a) you must explicitly compare, not just describe.
*Insufficient evidence* – quote the extracts and explain each quote.
*Lack of structure* – use paragraphs with clear topic sentences.

callouts.p: Students often write a single paragraph for part (a) instead of a structured comparison.

core.p: A visual guide to keep your comparison organised.
Think of comparing extracts like comparing two recipes for the same dish.
bullets: Both aim to produce a dish (the same theme).
Ingredients (language) differ: one uses simple spices, the other complex herbs.
Cooking method (structure) changes texture and flavour.
The final taste (tone) may be bitter or sweet depending on the recipe.
The analogy breaks down when the dishes are from completely different cuisines – you must still compare the core elements.

core.p: Use these to test your understanding and timing.
Remember:
bullets: Use the exact terminology the spec rewards.
Structure your comparison clearly – a table helps.
Quote and analyse both extracts.
Answer the related question with evidence and explanation.
Avoid common traps – plan, compare, and use precise language.

analogy.t: Comparing extracts is like comparing two recipes
analogy.p: Both aim to create a dish (theme). Ingredients (language) and cooking method (structure) differ, but the core goal remains. The analogy fails when the recipes are from entirely different cuisines – you still need to compare the fundamental elements.

terms.d: The words, phrases and stylistic devices used to convey meaning.
The organisation of the text, including paragraphing, dialogue and narrative sequence.
The underlying ideas or messages explored by the writer.
The way characters are presented and developed.
The writer’s attitude towards the subject.
The narrative perspective from which the story is told.
Sensory details that create mental pictures.
A reference to another text, event or cultural element.

mistakes.w: The text is about power
mistakes.r: The answer must analyse how power is portrayed, not just state it.

mistakes.w: I used the word ‘satire’ but didn’t explain it
mistakes.r: Explain the effect of satire on the reader.

mistakes.w: I compared only language
mistakes.r: Include structure, theme, characterisation, tone, and point of view.

mistakes.w: I quoted the extract but didn’t analyse
mistakes.r: Explain why the quote supports the point you’re making.

mistakes.w: I wrote one long paragraph
mistakes.r: Use separate paragraphs for each comparison point.

exam.q: Compare the extract from *Animal Farm* with an unseen modern extract of the same genre, focusing on how each text uses language and structure to convey its purpose.
model: Identify the purpose of each extract.
Analyse the language: diction, figurative language, rhetorical devices.
Examine the structure: paragraphing, narrative sequence, dialogue.
Discuss the themes and how each text treats them.
Conclude with a clear statement of similarity or difference.
exam.tip: Use a comparison table to keep points organised.

exam.q: Answer the following question on *Animal Farm*: How does Orwell use the character of Napoleon to explore the theme of power?
model: State the question’s focus: characterisation of Napoleon and theme of power.
Identify relevant passages where Napoleon’s actions illustrate power.
Explain how language (e.g. propaganda slogans) and structure (e.g. Napoleon’s speeches) support this.
Show how these devices reinforce the theme of power and corruption.
Conclude by linking back to the writer’s purpose.
exam.tip: Plan your answer: 1 paragraph for each point, 1 concluding paragraph.

exam.q: In the unseen modern extract, identify one rhetorical device and explain its effect on the reader.
model: Identify the device (e.g. hyperbole).
Explain its effect (e.g. exaggeration to emphasise urgency).
exam.tip: Quote the device and analyse its impact.

exam.q: Compare the tone of the *Animal Farm* extract with the unseen modern extract.
model: Describe the tone of each extract (e.g. satirical, critical).
Explain how the tone supports the purpose of each text.
exam.tip: Use adjectives like ‘grim’, ‘critical’ and justify with evidence.

exam.q: Explain how the structure of the *Animal Farm* extract contributes to its overall meaning.
model: Describe the structure (e.g. short paragraphs, clear narrative).
Analyse how this structure affects pacing and emphasis.
Link the structure to the writer’s purpose and the theme.
exam.tip: Look for paragraph breaks, dialogue, and narrative shifts.

worked.q: Write a model paragraph comparing the use of language in the *Animal Farm* extract and an unseen modern extract.
steps: 1. State the purpose of each extract.
2. Analyse diction and figurative language in each.
3. Explain how these choices support the purpose.
4. Conclude with a comparison sentence.
worked.ans: The *Animal Farm* extract uses simple, direct diction and irony to satirise the rise of tyranny, while the modern extract employs complex syntax and metaphor to critique social inequality. In both cases, the language choices heighten the reader’s awareness of power dynamics, but the *Animal Farm* text relies on stark, blunt imagery to convey its grim message, whereas the modern text uses subtle, layered metaphors to suggest that inequality is pervasive and insidious. Thus, while both texts aim to expose the corrupting influence of power, they differ in tone and intensity, reflecting their distinct historical contexts.

englit_ocr.2.2.summary: Animal Farm’s key characters—Napoleon, Snowball, Boxer, Squealer, Old Major, the pigs, and the other animals—are presented through Orwell’s use of allegorical naming, animal traits, speech patterns and narrative commentary. Their development mirrors the rise, corruption and eventual betrayal of the Soviet Revolution, showing how power corrupts and how propaganda manipulates the masses.

core.p: Napoleon the pig represents Stalin. He is presented as cunning, ruthless and increasingly tyrannical, using fear and propaganda to consolidate power.
bullets: Physical description: large, fierce-looking, often described as ‘large, rather fierce-looking’ (Chapter 5).
Speech: rarely speaks, but when he does his words are short, authoritative; later uses slogans like ‘Four legs good, two legs bad’.
Actions: drives the dogs, expels Snowball, rewrites commandments, trades with humans.
Symbolic devices: uses the dogs as a private army – allegory for secret police.
Narrative tone: Orwell’s detached narration highlights Napoleon’s hypocrisy (e.g., ‘the pigs had learned to read and write’).

callouts.p: Napoleon = Stalin; his rise shows how revolutionary ideals are subverted by personal ambition.

core.p: Snowball embodies Trotsky and the original revolutionary zeal. He is portrayed as intelligent, persuasive and innovative, but ultimately out‑maneuvered.
bullets: Physical description: ‘a brilliant white pig’ (Chapter 1).
Speech: eloquent, uses persuasive rhetoric – e.g., the windmill plan.
Ideas: proposes the windmill, promotes education, writes the Seven Commandments.
Downfall: scapegoated after Napoleon’s coup; later ‘executed’ by the dogs.
Narrative contrast: Orwell describes Snowball’s ideas as ‘bright’ but his removal shows the loss of democratic debate.

callouts.p: Snowball = Trotsky; his expulsion mirrors Trotsky’s exile.

core.p: Boxer the horse is the embodiment of the proletariat: hardworking, trusting, and ultimately betrayed.
bullets: Mottoes: ‘I will work harder’ and later ‘Napoleon is always right’.
Physical description: ‘large, strong, and tireless’.
Work ethic: leads the building of the windmill, never questions authority.
Tragic end: sold to the knacker when injured – a direct comment on Soviet exploitation of workers.
Narrative tone: sympathetic, highlighting the cruelty of the regime.

callouts.p: Boxer = the Soviet working class; his fate illustrates the betrayal of the revolution’s promises.

core.p: Squealer is the mouthpiece of the pigs, using persuasive language to manipulate the other animals.
bullets: Speech: uses ‘rhetorical questions’, ‘statistics’, and ‘repetition’ (e.g., ‘Surely there is no one among you who does not love the cause?’).
Techniques: euphemism (‘re‑education’), appeal to fear, and distortion of facts.
Role: rewrites the Seven Commandments, justifies trade with humans.
Physical description: ‘a small, white, fat pig’ – contrasts with his big influence.

callouts.p: Squealer = Soviet state media/propaganda.

core.p: Old Major provides the ideological spark for the rebellion, representing Marx/Lenin.
bullets: Speech: delivers the ‘Beasts of England’ anthem, outlines the principles of Animalism.
Physical description: ‘a large boar, very wise, with a huge shaggy mane’.
Legacy: his ideas are twisted by the pigs; the original commandments are altered.
Narrative function: his death marks the shift from idealism to power‑struggle.

callouts.p: Old Major = Marx/Lenin; his vision is corrupted by those who seize power.

core.p: The rest of the farm’s inhabitants stand for the general populace, showing varying degrees of awareness and compliance.
bullets: Pigs: become the ruling elite; gradually adopt human habits.
Dogs: represent the secret police; trained to enforce obedience.
Sheep: repeat slogans blindly – ‘Four legs good, two legs bad’.
Molluscs (e.g., Moses the raven): symbolize religion/ideology used to pacify.
Narrative tone: Orwell’s detached description shows their passivity and eventual disillusionment.

callouts.p: Do not treat the animals as mere ‘characters’; they function as social groups in the allegory.

core.h: Presentation Techniques – how Orwell builds character
core.p: Orwell uses a blend of allegorical naming, animal characteristics, speech patterns, and narrative commentary to present each character’s role in the political satire.
bullets: Allegorical naming – direct parallels to historical figures.
Animal traits – physical traits echo personality (e.g., pigs = greedy, dogs = loyal to master).
Narrative voice – third‑person omniscient, often ironic, exposing hypocrisy.
Language devices – repetition, slogans, euphemism, and rhetorical questions.
Structural positioning – key characters introduced early, then evolve with the plot.

callouts.p: When answering, link each character’s presentation to the wider theme of power and corruption.

analogy.t: Animal Farm as a theatrical troupe
analogy.p: Imagine the farm as a theatre company where each animal plays a role in a political drama: Napoleon is the director who hijacks the script, Snowball is the original playwright whose ideas are censored, Boxer is the stagehand who works tirelessly behind the scenes, and Squealer is the publicist who spins the reviews. The analogy breaks down because, unlike actors who can choose to quit, the animals are forced to stay on stage, reflecting the lack of agency in totalitarian societies.

terms.d: A narrative in which characters, events and settings symbolise real‑world people, ideas or historical events.
A literary technique that uses humour, irony or exaggeration to criticise and expose folly or vice.
Information, ideas or rumours deliberately spread to influence public opinion, often by distortion.
A contrast between what is said or appears and what is actually meant or happens.
A short, memorable phrase used to persuade or rally support.
The perspective from which a story is told; in Animal Farm it is a detached, omniscient narrator.
The way an author creates and develops a character through description, speech, actions and thoughts.
The use of symbols to represent ideas or qualities beyond their literal meaning.

mistakes.w: ‘Napoleon is a good leader because he protects the farm.’
mistakes.r: The mark scheme expects you to show how Napoleon’s leadership is presented as tyrannical through fear, propaganda and the alteration of the commandments.

mistakes.w: ‘Boxer is a hero because he works hard.’
mistakes.r: You must link Boxer’s hard work to the theme of exploitation and his eventual betrayal, not just praise his diligence.

mistakes.w: ‘All the animals are the same.’
mistakes.r: The exam expects you to differentiate groups (pigs, dogs, sheep, etc.) and explain their distinct symbolic functions.

mistakes.w: ‘Old Major’s ideas are unchanged throughout the novel.’
mistakes.r: You need to show how his original principles are corrupted by the pigs over time.

mistakes.w: ‘Squealer uses only lies.’
mistakes.r: Mark scheme looks for specific techniques (euphemism, statistics, rhetorical questions) rather than a blanket statement.

exam.q: Explain how Orwell presents Napoleon as a tyrannical leader (4 marks).
model: Identifies Napoleon’s physical description and its connotations (large, fierce‑looking).
Shows his use of the dogs as a private army to instil fear.
Analyses his manipulation of language via Squealer and the rewriting of the commandments.
Links these techniques to the theme of power corrupting.
exam.tip: Use specific textual evidence (e.g., ‘Napoleon was not a pig of the same sort as the others’).

exam.q: Compare the presentation of Boxer with that of the sheep, focusing on how each group responds to propaganda (6 marks).
model: Describes Boxer’s personal mottoes and his trust in Napoleon.
Shows the sheep’s repetitive slogans and blind repetition.
Analyses language used for Boxer (e.g., ‘I will work harder’) versus the sheep (repetition of ‘Four legs good…’).
Explains how both are manipulated but in different ways – Boxer through appeal to duty, sheep through mindless chant.
Links both to the theme of the masses being controlled.
exam.tip: Balance paragraph: start with Boxer, then sheep, finish with comparative link.

exam.q: Why does Orwell give Old Major a speech at the start of the novel? (2 marks)
model: To introduce the ideology of Animalism (the revolutionary ideal).
To set up the allegorical link to Marx/Lenin and provide a foil for later corruption.
exam.tip: Mention the ‘Beasts of England’ anthem as part of the presentation.

exam.q: How does Squealer’s use of language help him persuade the other animals? (4 marks)
model: Identifies rhetorical questions, statistics and euphemism.
Shows examples from the text (e.g., ‘Surely there is no one among you who does not love the cause?’).
Explains how these techniques create a sense of authority and inevitability.
Links to the theme of propaganda.
exam.tip: Quote and comment on at least two techniques.

exam.q: Discuss the significance of the pigs’ gradual adoption of human habits (6 marks).
model: Notes the chronological progression (walking on two legs, drinking alcohol, sleeping in beds).
Explains how Orwell uses physical description and symbolism to show moral decay.
Links to the theme of betrayal of revolutionary ideals.
Shows how the change reinforces the allegory of Soviet leadership becoming indistinguishable from the oppressors they overthrew.
exam.tip: Use the final line ‘The creatures outside looked from pig to man, and from man to pig…’ as evidence.

worked.q: Model paragraph: How is Napoleon presented as a dictator?
steps: Start with a topic sentence linking Napoleon to the theme of power.
Provide a physical description and its connotations.
Give evidence of his use of the dogs and the expulsion of Snowball.
Analyse the rewriting of the commandments and Squealer’s propaganda.
Conclude by linking these techniques to the overall message about tyranny.
worked.ans: Napoleon is presented as a dictatorial figure whose rise mirrors Stalin’s seizure of power. Orwell describes him as ‘large, fierce‑looking’, a physical cue that suggests dominance. He consolidates authority by training the dogs as a private army, using them to chase Snowball away—an act that instils fear and eliminates opposition. The pigs then rewrite the Seven Commandments, a manipulation carried out through Squealer’s persuasive propaganda, showing how language is twisted to justify tyranny. Through these techniques Orwell demonstrates that power corrupts, turning revolutionary ideals into oppression.
